intro: Adelaide's suburbs keep three old river red gums on this map. On Overbury Drive in Clarence Park a red gum stands in the middle of the road, about 200 years old by press reports. On Glynburn Road in Kensington Gardens a heritage-listed gum stands on the verge, more than 250 years old by the national big-tree register. In Rostrevor another grows beside a shallow stream. All three are free to see from public ground.
meta_description: Three river red gums in Adelaide's suburbs: the gum in the middle of Overbury Drive, the heritage gum on Glynburn Road, and one at Rostrevor.

trees.name: The Red Gum of the Rostrevor Creek
trees.age_estimate: about 200 years by a reader's estimate
trees.story:
A River Red Gum stands with its roots at the edge of a shallow stream at Rostrevor, in the eastern suburbs of Adelaide. A reader who photographed it for us puts it at about 200 years old. That is their estimate, not a ring count.

The photograph shows why it is worth the walk. The trunk is broad and straight, flaring at the foot into thick, knuckled roots that grip the bank, and the clear water runs over the stones of the stream bed just in front of them. Part way up, a long wound has healed into a rolled lip of bark, leaving the ridged wood bare in the middle. Paler gums lean over the grass behind.

River red gum, Eucalyptus camaldulensis, is the tree of Australian watercourses, and it is often found like this, with its feet at the water's edge. The species is known for living a very long time. Whether this one is two centuries old is for a tape and a specialist to say. What the picture settles is that it is a big, old-looking tree in a setting a visitor can walk to and stand in front of.

If you go, take shoes you do not mind getting wet.
trees.how_to_recognise: A broad River Red Gum with knuckled roots at the edge of a shallow, stony stream and a long healed wound up its trunk.

trees.name: The Red Gum of Glynburn Road
trees.age_estimate: more than 250 years by the big-tree register; about 300 by a 1984 council plaque; 300 to 500 by a reader's estimate

location.address: Road reserve beside 364 Glynburn Road, Kensington Gardens, South Australia

trees.story:
In February 2024 an aerial inspection found cavities and hollowing inside this river red gum, and the City of Burnside closed Glynburn Road so that arborists could cut back its crown. The council calls it a heritage-listed tree.

Its age is a matter of several estimates. A plaque the council placed beside it in September 1984, quoted in Burnside's list of state heritage places, says the "old gum tree" was a mature tree long before the colonisation of Australia, and gives it about 300 years, 29 metres of height and a girth of 10.4 metres. The National Register of Big Trees lists a remnant river red gum on Glynburn Road in Kensington Gardens at more than 250 years, 30.5 metres tall and 8.45 metres round, with a crown 18 metres wide. That entry gives no street number, so we take it to be this tree. The two girths do not agree, and we give both. The reader who sent it to us puts it at 300 to 500 years, by their estimate.

It stands on the road reserve beside 364 Glynburn Road in Kensington Gardens and is seen from the footpath. We have no photograph of it yet. If you pass, one taken from the path would give it a face here.
trees.how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its size, a river red gum about 30 metres tall and more than 8 metres round. It stands on the eastern verge of Glynburn Road, beside number 364.

trees.name: The Red Gum of Overbury Drive
trees.age_estimate: about 200 years, as press reports estimate

location.address: Overbury Drive, Clarence Park, South Australia

trees.story:
On Overbury Drive in Clarence Park, a quiet suburban street in Adelaide's inner south, a river red gum stands in the middle of the road and the tarmac bends around it. Press reports put it at about 200 years old and more than 20 metres tall. Residents call it the Sacred Tree, and it has become a symbol of holding out against urban spread.

Its position is the reason it is known. The photograph, taken at sunset, shows the pale, deeply furrowed trunk rising from the centre of the carriageway with power lines crossing in front and houses, parked cars and a few neighbours on either side. The crown spreads wide and green above it.

It has also been in trouble. After residents raised alarms about its decline, the City of Unley installed water bollards around the roots to deliver water to the tree, reported at about 1,600 litres a day, and said it would change the street to reduce stress on it. The age is an estimate, with no ring count, and the figures come from news coverage rather than a register.

It stands on a public street and costs nothing to see. Traffic uses the road, so look from the pavement.
trees.how_to_recognise: A big river red gum standing in the middle of the road on Overbury Drive, with the street curving around its trunk.

question_meta: A River Red Gum in Rostrevor, Adelaide, about 200 years old by a reader's estimate. Where it stands and how to see it.
question_answer: A reader-found River Red Gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis) stands beside a shallow stream in Rostrevor, in Adelaide's eastern suburbs. The reader who photographed it for us puts it at about 200 years old. It is free to see from the creek bank.
question_context: The age is a reader's estimate. No register lists the tree and no encyclopaedia article describes it, so nothing has been checked against a record, and nobody has published a tape measurement. The reader who photographed it for us gives the species as River Red Gum, Eucalyptus camaldulensis, the tree of Australian watercourses, which is often found standing with its roots at the water's edge as this one does. The photograph shows a broad, straight trunk flaring into thick roots over a stony stream bed, and a long wound part way up the trunk that has healed into a rolled lip of bark around bare, ridged wood. Paler gums lean over the grass behind it. River red gums are known for reaching great ages, but whether this one is two centuries old is for a tape and a specialist to say. What the picture settles is that it is a big, old-looking tree in a place a visitor can reach and stand in front of. The pin is the reader's own GPS fix at the tree.
